c.text: Our galaxy may hold about 100 million black holes
and almost none of them has ever been seen
They don't shine, they give off no light, they just drift silently in the dark
In 2022, scientists caught one of these lone black holes for the first time
wandering just 5,000 light-years from Earth
And that is only the first of the scariest places in the universe
By the last one, the question won't be how big the universe is, but how little of it we can see

c.text: A black hole is almost impossible to see: it gives off no light, it swallows it
So how did scientists catch one?
In 2011, a distant star suddenly grew brighter, for about 270 days, then faded back
Something had passed in front of it, and its gravity bent the star's light
just like a glass of water makes things behind it look bigger and bent
Hubble watched that spot for six years, and the numbers were clear
Something many times heavier than our Sun, and completely dark
No companion star, no galaxy centre: a lone black hole wandering through space
The good news: it isn't heading towards Earth
The bad news: black holes like this are almost impossible to spot in advance
If one ever came near our solar system, the first sign might be planets changing course
A black hole at least stays quiet. At the next place, the danger is light itself

c.text: 27 DECEMBER 2004
One night in December 2004, instruments on many satellites failed at once
The radiation was so strong their detectors were swamped, and Earth's upper atmosphere was shaken
It came from 50,000 light-years away, near the far side of our galaxy
There sits a magnetar: a dead star only 20 kilometres wide, yet heavier than our Sun
Its magnetic field is about a quadrillion times stronger than Earth's
It's said it could wipe a credit card from half the distance to the Moon
That night, a starquake struck the star
In a tenth of a second it released as much energy as our Sun does in 100,000 years
Even after crossing that distance it shook Earth, and that is what stunned scientists
Within 10 light-years, it could have stripped away much of Earth's ozone layer
A magnetar is still just a dead star. Some things outshine entire galaxies

c.text: In 1963, Dutch astronomer Maarten Schmidt was reading the light of a small blue dot
It looked exactly like a star
But as he understood its light, it turned out not to be a star at all
It was more than 2 billion light-years away, yet shining like a nearby star
Today these are called quasars
A huge black hole at a galaxy's centre, feeding right now
Gas swirls around it so fast that friction heats it to millions of degrees
so bright that a quasar outshines all the stars of its galaxy a thousand times
Luckily most quasars are billions of light-years away; their light left when the universe was young
And inside one of them hides one of the heaviest black holes ever found

c.text: It's called TON 618. In 1957, a survey in Mexico listed it as a faint blue star
Today its black hole is estimated at 40 to 66 billion times the mass of our Sun
So big that Neptune's whole orbit would fit inside it, more than twenty times over
Its light took more than 10 billion years to reach Earth
We see TON 618 as it was before Earth even existed
Every place so far could at least be seen. The next one, nobody can see
and right now it is pulling the entire Milky Way towards itself

c.text: Earth circles the Sun, and the Sun circles the galaxy: that much scientists knew
But between 1970 and 1980, something strange came to light
the Milky Way and thousands of nearby galaxies are all rushing in one direction
at about 600 km per second: Earth to the Moon in just 11 minutes
Something enormously heavy is pulling them all: scientists named it the Great Attractor
The problem: in that direction, our own galaxy's stars and dust block the view
like a pillar standing right in front of your eyes in a room
Behind that curtain lies a huge cluster of galaxies, but it can't pull that hard on its own
Further still is an even bigger cluster that may be pulling everything
In 2014 scientists mapped our whole region and named it Laniakea
In Hawaiian it means "immeasurable heaven"
In some places galaxies crowd and pull on each other, and in others there is nothing at all

c.text: In 1981, astronomer Robert Kirshner and his team were measuring galaxy distances when their numbers ran out
There were no galaxies, just an empty region 330 million light-years wide: the Boötes Void
A space that size should hold thousands of galaxies; scientists found about 60
Astronomer Greg Aldering said: if the Milky Way sat in this void, we wouldn't have known other galaxies existed until the 1960s
Beyond our own stars the night sky would be completely black: the Great Nothing
It probably formed as smaller voids merged: no mystery, just empty space
But in 2015 a far bigger empty region was found, one that may have marked the oldest light in the universe

c.text: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe cooled enough for light to travel freely
That light still arrives from every direction as microwaves, almost the same temperature everywhere
But in 2004 a patch of sky turned up that was too cold to be chance: the Cold Spot
In 2015 a team found a supervoid in that very direction, about 1.8 billion light-years across
But the numbers didn't add up: the void alone couldn't explain the cold
And here the story gets strange: some scientists suggested a wild idea
maybe the spot is the bruise of a collision with another universe, like two soap bubbles touching
Most scientists reject it, but nobody has the full answer to the Cold Spot yet
And the other-universe story doesn't end there: in 2008 some scientists thought they had measured its pull

c.text: Astronomer Alexander Kashlinsky's team measured the motion of huge galaxy clusters: hundreds seemed to flow one way
like leaves drifting down a river; they called it Dark Flow
The pull, they said, came from beyond the observable universe, from something no one can ever see
The news went round the world. Then in 2013 the Planck satellite checked again with far better data
and this time found no clear sign of a dark flow
Kashlinsky's team still stands by its result; most scientists think the flow was never there
Honestly, that is scary too: about the edge of the universe, we can only guess
And where exactly is that edge?

c.text: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old
Yet the edge of the part we can see is about 46 billion light-years away in every direction
because while the light travelled towards us, space itself kept expanding
What lies beyond that edge no one knows: more galaxies, or something completely different
Strangest of all, the view is shrinking, because space is expanding faster and faster
One by one, distant galaxies will vanish from view
In about 100 billion years, only our own galaxy will be left in the sky
An astronomer then would never learn there was a Big Bang, or billions of other galaxies
Maybe the scariest place isn't a void or a black hole, but the darkness slowly covering everything
And maybe humans arrived at just the right time, while there is still so much left to see
